q: A cyclist slows steadily from 15 m/s to 3.0 m/s in 4.0 s. What is the cyclist's acceleration?
w: a = (v - v0) / t = (3.0 - 15) / 4.0 = -12 / 4.0 = -3.0 m/s². The negative sign shows the cyclist is slowing.

n.0: Divides only the final speed by the time (3.0 / 4.0); acceleration uses the change in velocity.
n.2: Adds the speeds (15 + 3.0 = 18) instead of subtracting them.
n.3: Drops the sign; the velocity decreases, so the acceleration is opposite the motion (negative).

q: A train moves at a constant 72 km/h. How far does it travel in 15 s? (1 m/s = 3.6 km/h)
w: Convert first: 72 km/h / 3.6 = 20 m/s. Then d = v t = 20 x 15 = 300 m.

n.0: Converts correctly but slips a decimal place (20 x 1.5).
n.1: Multiplies 72 by 15 without converting km/h to m/s.
n.2: Multiplies by 3.6 instead of dividing (72 x 3.6 = 259 m/s), then by 15.

q: On a position-time graph, a cart's line is straight and slopes steadily upward. What does this show about the cart's motion?
o: It speeds up at a constant rate
It slows down at a constant rate
It is at rest at a fixed position
It moves at a constant velocity
w: The slope of a position-time graph is velocity. A straight line has a constant slope, so the velocity is constant.

n.0: Reads the slope of a position-time graph as acceleration; speeding up would make the line curve upward.
n.1: Slowing down would make the line curve and flatten, not stay straight.
n.2: A cart at rest gives a horizontal line, not a rising one.

q: A velocity-time graph for a scooter shows a straight line rising from 0 m/s at t = 0 to 12 m/s at t = 6.0 s. How far does the scooter travel in those 6.0 s?
w: Displacement = area under a v-t graph. The area is a triangle: 1/2 x 6.0 s x 12 m/s = 36 m.

n.0: Uses the full rectangle (6.0 x 12) and leaves out the 1/2 for a triangle.
n.2: Reads the final velocity off the graph instead of the area under it.
n.3: 2.0 is the slope (12 / 6.0 = 2.0 m/s²): the acceleration, not the distance.

q: A stone is dropped from rest off a bridge. Ignoring air resistance and using g = 10 m/s², how fast is it falling after 4.0 s?
w: From rest, v = g t = 10 x 4.0 = 40 m/s.

n.1: 80 is the distance fallen in meters (1/2 x 10 x 16), not the speed.
n.2: Divides g by t (10 / 4.0) instead of multiplying.
n.3: Squares the time (10 x 4.0²); speed grows linearly with time in free fall.

q: A set of keys falls from rest off a balcony and hits the ground 2.0 s later. Ignoring air resistance and using g = 10 m/s², how high is the balcony? (d = 1/2 gt²)

n.1: Doubles instead of halving: 2 x 10 x 4.0 = 80.
n.2: Leaves out the 1/2 (10 x 4.0 = 40).
n.3: Forgets to square t: 1/2 x 10 x 2.0 = 10.

q: A ball is thrown straight up. Ignoring air resistance and using g = 9.8 m/s², what are its velocity and acceleration at the highest point?
w: At the top the ball stops for an instant (v = 0), but gravity still acts, so the acceleration is g = 9.8 m/s² downward the whole time.

n.0: Gravity accelerates the ball downward, not upward, at every point of the flight.
n.1: Zero velocity is not zero acceleration; gravity keeps pulling the ball down.
n.3: Swaps the two: the velocity is momentarily zero while the acceleration is 9.8 m/s².

q: A 2.0 kg ball and a 6.0 kg ball are released together from the same height in a vacuum chamber. How does the acceleration of the 6.0 kg ball compare with that of the 2.0 kg ball?
w: In free fall with no air resistance every object accelerates at g, whatever its mass, so the accelerations are equal and the balls land together.

n.0: Inverts the mass ratio; mass does not change free-fall acceleration.
n.1: Squares the mass ratio; mass does not change free-fall acceleration.
n.3: Assumes heavier objects fall faster in proportion to mass; mass cancels in free fall.

q: From the same height and at the same instant, one ball is dropped and a second is thrown horizontally at 8.0 m/s. Ignoring air resistance, which lands first?
o: They land at the same time
It depends on the throwing speed
w: Horizontal and vertical motions are independent. Both balls start with zero vertical velocity and fall with g, so they hit the ground together.

n.1: The dropped ball does not fall faster; both have the same vertical motion.
n.2: Horizontal speed does not shorten the fall; it only carries the ball farther.
n.3: Throwing speed changes how far the ball travels sideways, not how long its vertical fall takes.

q: A ball is thrown horizontally at 8.0 m/s from a rooftop. Ignoring air resistance, which statement about its motion before it lands is correct?
o: Its acceleration points forward and down
Its horizontal velocity stays at 8.0 m/s
Its vertical velocity stays at zero
w: No horizontal force acts (ignoring air), so the horizontal velocity stays constant at 8.0 m/s while the ball falls with g.

n.0: The only acceleration is g, straight down; there is no forward acceleration.
n.2: With no air resistance there is no horizontal force to slow the ball.
n.3: Gravity gives the ball a growing downward velocity as soon as it leaves the roof.

q: A ball rolls off a lab bench 1.25 m high at 2.0 m/s. Using g = 10 m/s² and ignoring air resistance, how far from the bench does it land? (fall distance = 1/2 gt²)
w: Fall time: 1.25 = 1/2 x 10 x t², so t² = 0.25 and t = 0.50 s. Horizontal distance = 2.0 m/s x 0.50 s = 1.0 m.

n.0: Assumes a fall time of 1.0 s instead of solving for it.
n.2: Multiplies the speed by the height (2.0 x 1.25); distance needs the fall time.
n.3: Uses t² (0.25) as if it were t, giving 2.0 x 0.25 = 0.50 m.

q: A 1,500 kg car accelerates at 2.0 m/s². What net force acts on the car?
w: F_net = m a = 1,500 kg x 2.0 m/s² = 3,000 N.

n.0: Divides mass by acceleration (1,500 / 2.0); Newton's second law multiplies them.
n.1: Gives the mass value as if it were a force; it must be multiplied by the acceleration.
n.3: Computes the car's weight (1,500 x 10) instead of the net force for this acceleration.

q: An orderly pushes an 80 kg loaded stretcher with a 200 N horizontal force. Friction on the wheels totals 40 N. What is the stretcher's acceleration?
w: Net force = 200 N - 40 N = 160 N. a = F_net / m = 160 / 80 = 2.0 m/s².

n.1: Uses the applied force (200 / 80) instead of the net force; friction opposes the push.
n.2: Uses the friction force alone (40 / 80) as if it were the net force.
n.3: Adds friction to the push (240 / 80); friction acts against the motion.

q: An astronaut has a mass of 70 kg on Earth. On the Moon, where g = 1.6 m/s², what are her mass and weight?
w: Mass is the amount of matter and does not change: 70 kg. Weight W = m g = 70 x 1.6 = 112 N.

n.1: Swaps the values and units; mass is in kilograms and weight in newtons.
n.2: Mass does not shrink on the Moon; only weight changes.
n.3: 686 N is her weight on Earth (70 x 9.8), not on the Moon.

q: A 1,000 kg car collides head-on with a 2,000 kg truck. During the collision, how does the force the truck exerts on the car compare with the force the car exerts on the truck?
o: Equal in size and opposite in direction
The truck's force is twice as large
The car's force is twice as large
Equal in size and in the same direction
w: Newton's third law: the two objects exert equal and opposite forces on each other, whatever their masses. The car accelerates more because its mass is smaller.

n.1: The larger mass does not exert a larger force; the forces form an equal third-law pair.
n.2: The forces are equal; the smaller mass changes its motion more, but its force is not larger.
n.3: Action and reaction act in opposite directions, each on a different object.

q: A book rests on a table. According to Newton's third law, what is the reaction force to Earth's gravitational pull on the book?
o: The book's gravitational pull on Earth
The book's downward push on the table
The table's upward push on the book
The floor's upward push on the table
w: Third-law pairs are the same type of force acting on two different objects: Earth pulls the book down, so the book pulls Earth up with an equal force.

n.1: This is a contact force; its partner is the table's push on the book, not Earth's gravity.
n.2: The table's push balances the book's weight, but both act on the book, so they are not a third-law pair.
n.3: That push acts on the table and is a contact force; Earth's pull on the book pairs with the book's pull on Earth.

q: A delivery van travels along a straight, level highway at a constant 25 m/s. Which statement about the forces on the van is correct?
o: The forward force is larger than the drag
A net forward force keeps it moving
The drag is larger than the forward force
The net force on the van is zero
w: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so by F_net = m a the forces are balanced and the net force is zero (Newton's first law).

n.0: A forward force larger than drag would make the van speed up.
n.1: An object at constant velocity needs no net force to keep moving.
n.2: Drag larger than the forward force would give a net backward force and slow the van down.

q: A 30 kg crate slides across a level floor. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.25. Using g = 10 m/s², what friction force acts on it? (f = μN)
w: Normal force on a level floor = weight = m g = 30 x 10 = 300 N. f = μN = 0.25 x 300 = 75 N.

n.0: Multiplies μ by the mass (0.25 x 30) and leaves out g.
n.1: Divides the normal force by μ (300 / 0.25) instead of multiplying.
n.3: 300 N is the normal force; it must be multiplied by μ.

q: A nursing assistant finds that a heavy supply cart takes more force to start moving than to keep rolling at a steady speed. Which explains this?
o: The normal force drops once the cart moves
Maximum static friction exceeds kinetic friction
Kinetic friction exceeds maximum static friction
The cart's mass drops once it starts moving
w: Static friction (surfaces not yet sliding) usually has a larger maximum than kinetic friction, so starting motion takes more force than maintaining it.

n.0: On a level floor the normal force equals the weight whether the cart is moving or not.
n.2: Reverses the rule: static friction's maximum is the larger one.
n.3: Mass is the amount of matter; it does not change when the cart moves.

q: A brick slides across a floor first on its large face, then on its narrow edge. In the simple friction model, how does the kinetic friction compare?
o: It depends on the sliding speed
w: In the simple model f = μN: friction depends on the surfaces (μ) and the normal force, not on contact area or speed. The brick's weight is the same either way.

n.0: A smaller area does not change friction; the normal force is unchanged.
n.1: Kinetic friction in the simple model does not depend on speed.
n.3: Contact area does not change friction in the simple model.

q: The same net force acts on a 3.0 kg cart and on a 12 kg cart. How does the acceleration of the 3.0 kg cart compare with that of the 12 kg cart?
w: a = F / m. With the same force, a is inversely proportional to mass: 12 / 3.0 = 4, so the lighter cart accelerates 4 times as much.

n.0: Equal force does not mean equal acceleration when the masses differ.
n.2: Squares the mass ratio; a = F / m is a simple inverse relationship.
n.3: Treats acceleration as directly proportional to mass; it is inversely proportional.

q: What is the momentum of a 0.20 kg ball moving at 15 m/s?
w: p = m v = 0.20 kg x 15 m/s = 3.0 kg·m/s.

n.0: Computes kinetic energy (1/2 x 0.20 x 15² = 22.5 J), not momentum.
n.2: Halves the product as if momentum carried a 1/2 like kinetic energy.
n.3: Divides speed by mass (15 / 0.20) instead of multiplying.

q: A 0.50 kg ball moving at 20 m/s is caught and stopped in 0.25 s. What average force does the glove exert on the ball?
w: Change in momentum = 0.50 x 20 = 10 kg·m/s. Impulse F t = change in p, so F = 10 / 0.25 = 40 N.

n.0: Multiplies the momentum change by the time (10 x 0.25) instead of dividing.
n.1: Divides the speed by the time (20 / 0.25) and leaves out the mass.
n.2: 10 kg·m/s is the change in momentum, not the force.

q: Why does an air bag reduce injury to a driver in a crash?
o: It lengthens the stopping time, raising the impulse
It shortens the stopping time, lowering the force
It reduces the driver's change in momentum
It lengthens the stopping time, lowering the force
w: The driver's change in momentum is fixed by the crash. Impulse F t = change in p, so stretching the stopping time lowers the average force.

n.0: The impulse equals the change in momentum, which the air bag does not change.
n.1: A shorter stopping time would raise the force, not lower it.
n.2: The driver still goes from moving to stopped; the air bag changes the time, not the momentum change.

q: A 3,000 kg truck moving at 12 m/s strikes a stationary 1,000 kg car, and the two lock together. What is their speed just after the collision?
w: Momentum before = 3,000 x 12 = 36,000 kg·m/s. After, the mass is 4,000 kg: v = 36,000 / 4,000 = 9.0 m/s.

n.1: Divides the momentum by the car's mass alone; both vehicles move together.
n.2: Halves the speed by averaging; the masses are unequal, so use conservation of momentum.
n.3: Assumes the truck keeps its speed; the stuck-together mass is larger, so the speed drops.

q: A 5.0 kg rifle fires a 0.020 kg bullet at 500 m/s. What is the rifle's recoil speed?
w: Total momentum starts at zero. Bullet p = 0.020 x 500 = 10 kg·m/s, so the rifle has 10 kg·m/s backward: v = 10 / 5.0 = 2.0 m/s.

n.1: Divides the bullet's speed by the rifle's mass (500 / 5.0) and leaves out the bullet's mass.
n.2: Inverts the division (5.0 / 10).
n.3: Slips a decimal: uses 0.20 kg for the bullet (0.20 x 500 / 5.0).

q: Two cars collide and crumple, and some kinetic energy becomes heat and sound. Assuming no external forces act, which quantity is conserved?
w: In an inelastic collision of an isolated system, total momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not; some becomes heat, sound and deformation.

n.0: Both are conserved only in an elastic collision, where objects bounce without loss.
n.1: Reverses the rule: here kinetic energy is lost while momentum is kept.
n.2: Momentum is conserved in every collision of an isolated system.

q: A 2.0 kg cart moving east at 4.0 m/s collides with a 2.0 kg cart moving west at 1.0 m/s, and they stick together. What is their velocity afterward?
w: Take east as positive: total p = (2.0)(4.0) + (2.0)(-1.0) = 8.0 - 2.0 = 6.0 kg·m/s. v = 6.0 / 4.0 = 1.5 m/s, positive, so east.

n.1: Divides by one cart's mass (6.0 / 2.0); the joined mass is 4.0 kg.
n.2: Adds the momenta as if both carts moved east (10 / 4.0).
n.3: Gets the size right but the direction wrong; the eastward cart had more momentum.

q: A runner doubles her speed. By what factor do her momentum and her kinetic energy change?
w: p = m v is proportional to v, so it doubles. KE = 1/2 m v² is proportional to v², so it rises by 2² = 4.

n.1: Treats kinetic energy as linear in speed; it depends on v².
n.2: Swaps the two relationships; momentum is linear in v and kinetic energy goes with v².
n.3: Treats momentum as depending on v²; p = m v is linear.

q: A patient in a gait study pushes against a force plate with an average force of 300 N for 0.40 s. What impulse does she deliver?
w: Impulse J = F t = 300 N x 0.40 s = 120 N·s.

n.1: Divides force by time (300 / 0.40) instead of multiplying.
n.2: Slips a decimal place (300 x 4.0).
n.3: Halves the product; impulse has no 1/2 factor.

q: Which collision is closest to perfectly elastic?
o: A lump of wet clay sticking to a brick wall
Gas molecules bouncing off one another
A car crumpling into a barrier
w: In an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. Collisions between gas molecules are treated as elastic.

n.0: Objects that stick together are perfectly inelastic: the largest kinetic energy loss.
n.2: Crumpling turns kinetic energy into deformation, heat and sound: inelastic.
n.3: Coupled train cars move off together: a perfectly inelastic collision.

q: A child rides a carousel horse that moves in a circle at a constant speed. What is the direction of the horse's acceleration?
o: Away from the center of the circle
There is none, since its speed is constant
Toward the center of the circle
Along the tangent, in the direction of motion
w: In uniform circular motion the velocity keeps changing direction, so the object accelerates toward the center (centripetal acceleration).

n.0: Centripetal means center-seeking; the outward 'centrifugal' feeling is inertia, not an acceleration.
n.1: Constant speed is not constant velocity; the changing direction is an acceleration.
n.3: A tangential acceleration would change the speed, which stays constant here.

q: An athlete swings a hammer (a ball on a cable) in a horizontal circle and lets go. Viewed from above, which path does the ball take just after release?
o: A straight line tangent to the circle
A curve that keeps circling the athlete
w: Once the inward tension is gone, no net horizontal force acts, so the ball keeps its velocity at release: a straight line along the tangent.

n.1: With the cable released, nothing pulls the ball inward.
n.2: There is no outward force to push it along the radius; inertia carries it along the tangent.
n.3: Circling needs a continuing inward force, which ended at release.

q: A runner moves around a curved section of track of radius 50 m at 5.0 m/s. What is her centripetal acceleration? (a_c = v²/r)

n.0: Divides r by v (50 / 5.0) instead of using v² / r.
n.1: Inverts the formula (50 / 25).
n.3: Forgets to square v (5.0 / 50).

q: A 1,200 kg car rounds a curve of radius 60 m at 15 m/s. What centripetal force must friction supply? (F_c = mv²/r)

n.0: Forgets to square v (1,200 x 15 / 60).
n.2: Leaves out the division by r (1,200 x 225).
n.3: Computes the momentum m v (1,200 x 15), not the force.

q: A cyclist takes the same curve at twice her earlier speed. By what factor does the centripetal force needed change?
w: F_c = m v² / r depends on v², so doubling v multiplies the force by 2² = 4.

n.0: Faster on the same curve needs more inward force, not less.
n.1: Treats the force as proportional to v; it depends on v².
n.2: The force depends on speed; a faster turn needs more grip.

q: Two objects attract each other with a gravitational force of 72 N. If the distance between their centers is tripled, what is the new force?
w: Gravity is inverse-square: tripling r divides the force by 3² = 9. 72 / 9 = 8.0 N.

n.0: Multiplies by 9; the square is right but the force must decrease.
n.2: Uses an inverse (1/r) relationship; gravity follows 1/r².
n.3: Multiplies by 3; a greater distance weakens the force.

q: Two objects attract each other with gravitational force F. If one mass is doubled and the distance between their centers is halved, what is the new force?
w: F is proportional to m1 m2 / r². Doubling one mass gives x2; halving r gives x(2²) = x4. Together: 2 x 4 = 8F.

n.1: Counts only the x4 from halving r and leaves out the x2 from doubling one mass.
n.2: Treats halving r as halving the force, cancelling the doubled mass.
n.3: Squares both changes; the mass factor is not squared.

q: A nurse pushes on a door with a 40 N force applied perpendicular to the door, 0.75 m from the hinges. What torque does she produce?
w: Torque τ = r F (force perpendicular) = 0.75 m x 40 N = 30 N·m.

n.0: Divides the force by the distance (40 / 0.75).
n.1: Halves the correct product; torque has no 1/2 factor.
n.3: Gives the force alone; torque also depends on the lever-arm distance.

q: A lab centrifuge rotor turns 50 times each second. What are its frequency and period?
w: Frequency = revolutions per second = 50 Hz. Period T = 1 / f = 1 / 50 = 0.020 s.

n.0: Swaps frequency and period.
n.2: The period is the reciprocal of the frequency, not equal to it.
n.3: Slips a decimal place in 1 / 50.

q: Astronauts aboard a space station orbiting Earth float freely inside the cabin. What is the best explanation?
o: Earth's gravity does not reach that altitude
The vacuum of space removes their weight
They and the station are in continuous free fall
w: Gravity still acts strongly at orbital height. The astronauts and the station fall around Earth together, so the astronauts press on nothing and feel weightless.

n.0: Gravity still acts at orbital height; it supplies the centripetal force that keeps the station in orbit.
n.1: Weight comes from gravity, not air; a vacuum does not remove it.
n.3: Centrifugal force is not a real force in this frame; gravity is the inward force keeping them in orbit.

q: A nursing assistant pushes a supply cart 12 m along a hallway with a steady 25 N force in the direction of motion. How much work does she do on the cart?
w: W = F d (force along the motion) = 25 N x 12 m = 300 J.

n.0: Halves the product; W = F d has no 1/2 factor.
n.1: Divides force by distance (25 / 12); work multiplies them.
n.2: Slips a decimal place (25 x 120).

q: A server carries a 20 N tray 5.0 m across a level room at constant speed, holding it up with a 20 N upward force. How much work does the upward holding force do on the tray?
w: Work is done only by a force component along the motion. The holding force is vertical and the motion is horizontal, so it does no work: 0 J.

n.1: Divides the force by the distance; and a perpendicular force does no work.
n.2: Halves 20 x 5.0; a force perpendicular to the motion does no work.
n.3: Multiplies the force by the distance even though the force is perpendicular to the motion.

q: What is the kinetic energy of a 60 kg jogger running at 3.0 m/s?

n.0: Leaves out the 1/2 (60 x 9.0).
n.2: Computes momentum (60 x 3.0 = 180 kg·m/s), not kinetic energy.
n.3: Forgets to square v (1/2 x 60 x 3.0).

q: A car's speed increases from 10 m/s to 30 m/s. By what factor does its kinetic energy increase?
w: KE is proportional to v². The speed triples, so KE rises by 3² = 9.

n.0: Cubes the speed ratio; the exponent on v is 2.
n.1: Doubles the speed ratio instead of squaring it.
n.2: Treats KE as proportional to v; it goes with v².

q: A 4.0 kg box is lifted onto a shelf 1.5 m high. Using g = 9.8 m/s², how much gravitational potential energy does it gain? (PE = mgh)

n.0: Adds a 1/2 that belongs to kinetic energy, not potential energy.
n.1: Leaves out g (4.0 x 1.5).
n.2: Leaves out the height: 4.0 x 9.8 = 39.2 N is the box's weight.

q: A ball is dropped from a height of 20 m. Ignoring air resistance and using g = 10 m/s², how fast is it moving just before it hits the ground?
w: PE at the top becomes KE at the bottom: m g h = 1/2 m v², so v² = 2 g h = 2 x 10 x 20 = 400 and v = 20 m/s.

n.1: Uses v² = g h (200) and drops the 2 from 1/2 m v².
n.2: Halves the correct speed; the energy equation gives 20 m/s.
n.3: Gives g h = 200 without the 2 or the square root.

q: An elevator motor lifts a 500 kg load 12 m in 20 s at constant speed. Using g = 10 m/s², what is its average power output?

n.1: Leaves out the height: 500 x 10 / 20 = 250.
n.2: 60,000 J is the work done; power divides it by the time.
n.3: Leaves out g: 500 x 12 / 20 = 300.

q: An electric motor uses 2,500 J of electrical energy to do 2,000 J of useful work. What is its efficiency?
w: Efficiency = useful output / input x 100% = 2,000 / 2,500 x 100% = 80%.

n.0: 20% is the share wasted (500 / 2,500), not the efficiency.
n.1: Divides the wasted 500 J by the 2,000 J output.
n.3: Inverts the ratio; efficiency cannot exceed 100%.

q: A lever has an effort arm of 1.2 m and a load arm of 0.30 m. Ideally, what effort force will lift a 600 N load?
w: Ideal mechanical advantage = effort arm / load arm = 1.2 / 0.30 = 4. Effort = 600 / 4 = 150 N (moved 4 times as far).

n.0: Multiplies the load by the mechanical advantage instead of dividing.
n.1: Multiplies the load by the load arm (600 x 0.30).
n.3: Assumes the lever gives no advantage; the longer effort arm cuts the force needed.

q: When the biceps contracts to flex the elbow and lift a cup held in the hand, which describes the lever?
w: The elbow is the fulcrum, the biceps pulls on the forearm between the elbow and the hand (effort in the middle) and the cup is the load: a third-class lever. The effort arm is much shorter than the load arm, so the mechanical advantage is below 1; the forearm gains speed and range of motion instead.

n.0: A first-class lever has the fulcrum between the effort and the load; the elbow is at one end of the forearm.
n.1: In a second-class lever the load sits between the fulcrum and the effort; here the cup is at the far end of the forearm.
n.2: Right class, but the biceps attaches close to the elbow, so the effort arm is shorter than the load arm and the mechanical advantage is below 1.

q: A 250 g stone displaces 100 mL of water when fully submerged. What is the stone's density, and does it float in water (1.0 g/mL)?
w: Density = m / V = 250 g / 100 mL = 2.5 g/mL. That is greater than water's 1.0 g/mL, so the stone sinks.

n.0: Inverts the formula (100 / 250); density is mass divided by volume.
n.1: The density is right, but an object denser than the fluid sinks.
n.3: Inverts the formula, and a density below 1.0 g/mL would float.

q: A 720 N person stands on both feet with a total sole area of 0.030 m². What pressure do the feet exert on the floor?

n.0: Multiplies force by area (720 x 0.030); pressure divides force by area.
n.2: 48,000 Pa would be the pressure on one foot (half the area).
n.3: Halves the answer; both feet share the weight, but the area already includes both.

q: Why does a sharp needle pierce skin more easily than a blunt one pushed with the same force?
o: A larger area gives a greater pressure
A smaller area gives a greater force
A smaller area gives less friction
A smaller area gives a greater pressure
w: P = F / A. With the same force, the needle's tiny tip area produces a much greater pressure.

n.0: A larger area spreads the force and lowers the pressure.
n.1: The force is the same for both needles; it is the pressure that rises.
n.2: Piercing depends on pressure at the tip, not on friction.

q: How much greater is the water pressure 5.0 m below the surface of a pool than at the surface? Use P = ρgh, ρ = 1,000 kg/m³ and g = 10 m/s².
w: Extra pressure = ρ g h = 1,000 x 10 x 5.0 = 50,000 Pa (about half an atmosphere).

n.0: Slips a decimal place (1,000 x 10 x 50).
n.1: Leaves out g (1,000 x 5.0).
n.3: Divides density by depth (1,000 / 5.0).

q: Three containers of different shapes and volumes are filled with water to the same depth. How does the water pressure at the bottom of each compare?
o: Greatest in the one holding most water
w: Fluid pressure depends only on density, g and depth (P = ρ g h), not on the container's shape or the total volume.

n.0: Width does not change pressure at a given depth.
n.1: Total volume does not set the pressure; depth does.
n.2: A narrow container does not concentrate the pressure; depth alone sets it.

q: In a hydraulic lift, a 150 N force pushes on an input piston of area 0.020 m². The output piston has an area of 0.80 m². What force does the output piston exert? (F1/A1 = F2/A2)

n.0: Pressure is transmitted, not force; the larger piston gets a larger force.
n.1: 150 / 0.020 = 7,500 is the pressure in pascals, not the output force; multiply it by the 0.80 m² area.
n.2: Inverts the area ratio (150 x 0.020 / 0.80); the larger piston gives the larger force.

q: Which statement about an ideal hydraulic lift is correct?
o: It multiplies energy, so less work is put in
It multiplies force; the small piston moves farther
It multiplies force and the work done
It multiplies force; the large piston moves farther
w: Pascal's principle transmits the pressure, so the large piston gets a large force. Work in = work out, so the small piston must move a longer distance.

n.0: Energy is conserved; hydraulics cannot multiply energy.
n.2: A hydraulic lift multiplies force, not work.
n.3: The large piston moves a shorter distance; that is the price of the larger force.

q: A sealed container displaces 0.0030 m³ of water when held fully under. It weighs 24 N. Using ρ_water = 1,000 kg/m³ and g = 10 m/s², what is the buoyant force on it, and what happens when it is released?
o: 30 N; it rises to the surface
30 N; it sinks to the bottom
3.0 N; it sinks to the bottom
24 N; it stays where it is
w: Buoyant force = weight of water displaced = 1,000 x 0.0030 x 10 = 30 N. That exceeds the 24 N weight, so the container rises and floats.

n.1: The buoyant force is right, but 30 N up beats 24 N down, so it rises.
n.2: Leaves out g (1,000 x 0.0030 = 3.0), then compares the wrong value.
n.3: Sets the buoyant force equal to the weight; that is true only once it floats at rest.

q: A block of wood with a density of 700 kg/m³ floats in fresh water (1,000 kg/m³). What fraction of its volume is below the waterline?
w: Fraction submerged = ρ_object / ρ_fluid = 700 / 1,000 = 0.70 = 70%.

n.0: 30% is the fraction above the waterline.
n.1: Half would be submerged only for a density of 500 kg/m³.
n.2: A block less dense than water floats partly above the surface.

q: A loaded cargo ship weighing 2.0 × 10^8 N floats at rest in a harbor. What weight of water does it displace?
o: The weight of its steel hull
w: A floating object displaces its own weight of fluid: the buoyant force (weight of water displaced) balances the ship's 2.0 × 10^8 N weight.

n.0: More buoyant force than weight would push the ship higher until they balance.
n.1: The displaced water balances the whole loaded ship, not the hull alone.
n.2: Less buoyant force than weight would make the ship sink.

q: A sound wave travels through air at 340 m/s with a frequency of 850 Hz. What is its wavelength? (v = fλ)

n.0: Inverts the formula (850 / 340).
n.1: Slips a decimal place (0.40 x 10).
n.3: Slips a decimal place the other way (0.40 / 10).

q: A wave has a period of 0.25 s and a wavelength of 3.0 m. What is its speed?

n.0: Multiplies wavelength by the period instead of the frequency.
n.1: Divides the period by the wavelength (0.25 / 3.0).
n.3: 4.0 Hz is the frequency; it must be multiplied by the wavelength.

q: A sonar pulse returns to a boat 0.40 s after it is sent toward the seafloor. Sound travels at 1,500 m/s in seawater. How deep is the water?
w: Total path = 1,500 x 0.40 = 600 m, down and back. Depth = 600 / 2 = 300 m.

n.0: Divides speed by time (1,500 / 0.40) instead of multiplying.
n.1: Forgets to halve: 600 m is the round trip.
n.3: Halves twice; the 600 m round trip is halved once.

q: As a sound wave travels through air, how do the air molecules move?
o: Along with the wave from source to listener
In circles around the wave's direction
Up and down, perpendicular to the wave
Back and forth, parallel to the wave
w: Sound is a longitudinal wave: molecules vibrate back and forth along the direction of travel, forming compressions and rarefactions.

n.0: Waves carry energy, not matter; the molecules stay near their rest positions.
n.1: Circular motion of particles describes surface water waves, not sound.
n.2: Perpendicular motion describes a transverse wave such as light or a wave on a string.

q: Which list ranks the speed of sound from fastest to slowest?
w: Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases: steel, water, air.

n.0: Liquids carry sound faster than gases.
n.1: Solids carry sound faster than liquids.
n.2: Reverses the order; sound is slowest in gases.

q: A musician plays the same note more loudly. Which property of the sound wave increases?
w: Loudness depends on amplitude (energy). The same note keeps the same frequency, so pitch is unchanged.

n.0: Wavelength is fixed by the frequency and the speed, neither of which changes.
n.1: Frequency sets pitch; the same note keeps the same frequency.
n.3: The speed of sound is set by the medium, not by loudness.

q: The frequency of a sound traveling in air is doubled. What happens to its wavelength and speed?
w: The medium sets the speed. With v fixed in v = f λ, doubling f halves λ.

n.0: The speed stays the same; only the wavelength changes.
n.1: Wavelength and frequency are inversely related at a fixed speed.
n.2: Changing frequency does not change wave speed in the same medium.

q: An ambulance with its siren on approaches a pedestrian, passes her and drives away. What does she hear?
o: A lower pitch as it nears, then a higher pitch
The siren's true pitch, growing louder then softer
A higher pitch both as it nears and as it leaves
A higher pitch as it nears, then a lower pitch
w: Doppler effect: a source moving toward an observer is heard at a higher frequency, and a source moving away at a lower frequency.

n.0: Reverses the Doppler effect; approaching raises the pitch.
n.1: Loudness does change, but so does the heard pitch: higher, then lower.
n.2: The pitch drops once the ambulance moves away.

q: A sound at 70 dB is compared with a sound at 50 dB. How many times greater is the intensity of the louder sound?
w: Each +10 dB multiplies intensity by 10. A 20 dB difference is two steps: 10 x 10 = 100 times.

n.0: Divides 70 by 50; decibel levels are not compared as a simple ratio.
n.1: Treats the 20 dB difference as a 20-fold change; decibels are logarithmic.
n.2: Treats 20 dB as a doubling; each 10 dB step is a tenfold change.

q: Noise-canceling headphones make a sound wave that meets incoming noise crest to trough. Which wave behavior does this use?
w: When a crest meets a trough the amplitudes cancel: destructive interference.

n.0: Diffraction is spreading around obstacles or through openings.
n.1: Resonance builds amplitude by driving an object at its natural frequency.
n.3: Constructive interference adds crests to crests and makes the sound louder.

q: Which list orders electromagnetic waves from lowest to highest frequency?
w: The spectrum by rising frequency: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma.

n.0: Swaps infrared and ultraviolet; infrared is below visible light, ultraviolet above.
n.1: Runs from highest to lowest frequency (reversed).
n.3: Swaps gamma and ultraviolet; gamma rays have the highest frequency.

q: Which type of electromagnetic radiation, used to make radiographs, carries more energy per photon than ultraviolet light?
w: Photon energy rises with frequency. X-rays lie above ultraviolet in frequency, so each photon carries more energy (and is ionizing).

n.0: Visible light has a lower frequency than ultraviolet.
n.2: Infrared has a lower frequency than ultraviolet, so less energy per photon.
n.3: Microwaves sit near the low-frequency end of the spectrum.

q: In a vacuum, how does the speed of radio waves compare with the speed of X-rays?
o: Each speed is set by the wavelength
They travel at the same speed
w: All electromagnetic waves travel at c = 3.00 × 10^8 m/s in a vacuum; they differ in frequency and wavelength, not speed.

n.0: Wavelength and frequency change together (c = f λ) while the speed stays c.
n.2: Higher frequency does not mean higher speed in a vacuum.
n.3: Longer wavelength does not mean higher speed in a vacuum.

q: Compared with violet light, red light has:
o: a shorter wavelength and lower frequency
a shorter wavelength and higher frequency
a longer wavelength and lower frequency
a longer wavelength and higher frequency
w: Red is at the long-wavelength, low-frequency end of visible light; violet is at the short-wavelength, high-frequency end.

n.0: Red does have the lower frequency, but its wavelength is longer than violet's, not shorter.
n.1: Describes violet compared with red (reversed).
n.3: Red does have the longer wavelength, but its frequency is lower than violet's, not higher.

q: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at 35° measured from the mirror's surface. What is the angle of reflection measured from the normal?
w: Angles are measured from the normal: 90° - 35° = 55° of incidence, and the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence: 55°.

n.1: 110° is the angle between the incident and reflected rays (55° + 55°), not the angle of reflection from the normal.
n.2: Doubles the surface angle; the law compares the incidence and reflection angles, both from the normal.
n.3: 35° is measured from the surface; the law of reflection uses the normal.

q: A dental assistant stands 1.5 m in front of a flat wall mirror. How far is she from her image, and what kind of image is it?
w: A plane mirror image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front (1.5 m), so she is 1.5 + 1.5 = 3.0 m from it. It is virtual and upright.

n.0: 1.5 m is the image's distance behind the mirror, not her distance from the image.
n.1: Plane mirror images are virtual and upright, not real and inverted.
n.2: The image is virtual (no light actually reaches it), and 3.0 m from her.

q: Store security mirrors and passenger-side car mirrors are convex. What kind of image do they form?
w: A convex (diverging) mirror forms a virtual, upright, smaller image, giving a wide field of view.

n.1: Convex mirrors do not form real, inverted images.
n.2: Convex mirror images are virtual and smaller.
n.3: Convex mirrors shrink the image; a magnified upright image comes from a concave mirror.

q: Light passes from air into glass. Which change occurs?
o: Its speed falls and it bends toward the normal
Its speed rises and it bends toward the normal
Its speed falls and it bends away from the normal
Its frequency falls and it bends toward the normal
w: Glass has a higher index of refraction, so light slows down and bends toward the normal. Its frequency stays the same; its wavelength shortens.

n.1: Light slows down in glass; it does not speed up.
n.2: Slowing down bends light toward the normal, not away from it.
n.3: Frequency does not change on refraction; speed and wavelength do.

q: Light enters a plastic with an index of refraction of 1.5. Using c = 3.0 × 10^8 m/s, what is the speed of light in the plastic? (n = c/v)

n.0: Multiplies c by n; light slows down in a material.
n.2: Divides c by 2 instead of by the index of 1.5.
n.3: 3.0 × 10^8 m/s is the speed in a vacuum; light is slower in plastic.

q: A student can read her textbook clearly but cannot see the whiteboard at the front of the room. Which condition does she have, and which lens corrects it?
w: Clear near vision with blurry distance vision is nearsightedness (myopia). A concave (diverging) lens corrects it.

n.0: Farsighted people see distant objects well; she sees near objects well.
n.1: She sees near objects well, so she is nearsighted, not farsighted.
n.2: Nearsightedness is right, but a converging lens corrects farsightedness.

q: A rubber rod rubbed with fur becomes negatively charged. What happened?
o: Friction created new charge on the rod
Electrons moved from the rod to the fur
Electrons moved from the fur to the rod
Protons moved from the rod to the fur
w: Rubbing transfers electrons. The rod gained electrons (negative) and the fur lost the same number (positive). Charge is conserved.

n.0: Charge is conserved: rubbing moves electrons but does not create charge.
n.1: Losing electrons would make the rod positive, not negative.
n.3: Protons stay in the nuclei; only electrons move when objects are charged.

q: Two small charged spheres repel each other with a force of 16 N. If the distance between them is doubled, what is the new force?
w: Coulomb's law is inverse-square: doubling r divides the force by 2² = 4. 16 / 4 = 4.0 N.

n.0: Multiplies by 2; a greater distance weakens the force.
n.2: Uses 1/r instead of 1/r²; doubling the distance quarters the force.
n.3: Multiplies by 4; the factor is right but the force must decrease.

q: A negatively charged balloon is held near a small piece of neutral paper, and the paper jumps toward it. Why?
o: The balloon transfers protons to the paper
Like charges attract at very short range
The paper already carries a hidden positive charge
The balloon polarizes the paper and attracts it
w: The balloon's negative charge pushes the paper's electrons slightly away, leaving the near side positive. The nearer positive side is attracted more strongly than the far side is repelled.

n.0: Protons do not move between objects; the balloon's field shifts the paper's electrons.
n.1: Like charges repel at every distance.
n.2: The paper is neutral; the attraction comes from charge separation within it.

q: Which statement about electric field lines is correct?
o: They point toward positive and away from negative charges
They point away from both positive and negative charges
They point away from positive and toward negative charges
They are spaced farther apart where the field is stronger
w: Field lines show the direction of force on a positive test charge: away from positive charges, toward negative charges. Closer lines mean a stronger field.

n.0: Reverses the direction of the field lines.
n.1: A positive test charge is pulled toward a negative charge, so lines point into it.
n.3: Closer, not farther, spacing shows a stronger field.

q: A 9.0 V battery is connected across a 3.0 Ω resistor. What current flows? (V = IR)

n.0: Subtracts R from V; Ohm's law divides.
n.2: Multiplies V by R; Ohm's law gives I = V / R.
n.3: Inverts the formula (R / V).

q: Resistors of 4.0 Ω, 6.0 Ω and 10 Ω are connected in series to a 40 V battery. What is the voltage across the 10 Ω resistor?
w: Series total R = 4.0 + 6.0 + 10 = 20 Ω. I = 40 / 20 = 2.0 A (the same through each). V across 10 Ω = 2.0 x 10 = 20 V.

n.0: 40 V is the whole battery voltage; series resistors share it.
n.2: Splits the voltage equally (40 / 3); series voltages divide in proportion to resistance.
n.3: 2.0 A is the current, not the voltage across the resistor.

q: A 4.0 Ω resistor and a 12 Ω resistor are connected in parallel. What is their combined resistance?
w: 1/R = 1/4.0 + 1/12 = 3/12 + 1/12 = 4/12, so R = 12/4 = 3.0 Ω (less than the smallest branch).

n.0: Stops at 1/R = 1/3 and forgets to take the reciprocal.
n.1: Adds the resistances as if they were in series.
n.2: Averages the two; a parallel total is less than the smallest resistor.

q: A 1,200 W hair dryer runs on a 120 V circuit. What current does it draw, and how much energy does it use in 0.50 h?

n.0: Inverts P / V (120 / 1,200).
n.1: Uses 1,200 W x 0.50 h = 600 Wh but labels it kWh.
n.3: Divides power by time (1,200 / 0.50) instead of multiplying.

q: In a home, one lamp burns out but the other lamps on the same circuit stay lit. What does this show?
o: The lamps are wired in parallel
The current is used up in each lamp
The burned-out lamp had the least resistance
The lamps are wired in series
w: In a parallel circuit each lamp has its own branch, so one open branch leaves the others working. Household wiring is parallel.

n.1: Current is not used up; it flows around the complete loop.
n.2: A lamp's resistance does not explain the others staying lit; separate branches do.
n.3: In series one break opens the only path and every lamp goes out.

q: Which change to a copper wire lowers its resistance?
o: Using a thicker wire of the same length
Using a thinner wire of the same length
Heating the wire to a higher temperature
Using a longer wire of the same thickness
w: Resistance falls as cross-sectional area rises: a thicker wire offers more paths for current.

n.1: A thinner wire has more resistance.
n.2: A metal's resistance rises with temperature.
n.3: Resistance rises with length.

q: A student wants a coil electromagnet to lift heavier iron objects. Which change would make it stronger?
o: Increase the number of turns in the coil
Use thinner wire carrying less current
Replace the iron core with an aluminum one
Reverse the direction of the current
w: An electromagnet gets stronger with more turns, more current and an iron core.

n.1: Less current weakens the electromagnet.
n.2: Aluminum is not ferromagnetic; an iron core strengthens the field.
n.3: Reversing the current swaps the poles but does not change the strength.

q: A bar magnet is cut in half across its middle. What results?
o: One piece with a north pole, one with a south pole
Two pieces of iron with no magnetic poles
One magnet and one unmagnetized piece
Two magnets, each with a north and a south pole
w: Magnetic poles always come in pairs. Each piece becomes a smaller magnet with its own north and south pole.

n.0: Isolated north or south poles do not exist; each piece has both.
n.1: The pieces stay magnetized; cutting does not remove the poles.
n.2: Both pieces stay magnetized, each with a north and a south pole.

q: A bar magnet rests motionless inside a wire coil connected to a meter. What does the meter show, and what happens as the magnet is pulled out?
o: Steady current; the current stops as it moves
Steady current; the current reverses as it moves
No current; a current flows as it moves
No current; still no current as it moves
w: Induction needs a changing magnetic field through the coil. A still magnet induces nothing; moving it changes the field and induces a current.

n.0: A steady, unchanging field induces no current.
n.1: A stationary magnet induces no current to begin with.
n.3: Pulling the magnet out changes the field through the coil, so current flows.

q: Which device converts mechanical energy into electrical energy?
w: A generator turns a coil in a magnetic field (or a magnet near a coil), inducing current: mechanical to electrical.

n.0: An electromagnet uses current to make a magnetic field; it does not produce electricity.
n.1: A motor does the reverse: electrical to mechanical.
n.2: A transformer changes AC voltage; it converts electrical energy to electrical energy.

q: Why does a transformer work with alternating current but not with steady direct current?
o: Direct current demagnetizes the iron core
Alternating current makes a stronger steady field
Direct current cannot flow through copper coils
It needs a changing magnetic field to induce voltage
w: A transformer works by induction: the changing current in one coil makes a changing field that induces voltage in the other. Steady DC makes a steady field, which induces nothing.

n.0: DC does not demagnetize the core; its unchanging field simply induces no voltage.
n.1: AC is useful here because its field changes, not because it is stronger.
n.2: DC flows through copper coils easily; the problem is that its field does not change.
